# Decoding Internal Combustion Diagnostics: Pressure vs. Compression

When a shop diagnoses a blown head gasket solely because your cooling system loses pressure while compression tests look pristine, it is often a case of misinterpreting the physics of internal combustion engines. In your specific scenarioâa Mazda MX-5 with 175 psi compression across all cylinders, no external leaks, but a cooling system that fails to hold pressure after an overheating eventâthe data points are telling a nuanced story that requires separating two distinct failure modes: mechanical integrity versus sealing integrity.

Compression numbers measure the ability of the cylinder head gasket and piston rings to seal the combustion chamber against high pressure during the power stroke. A consistent 175 psi across all cylinders indicates that the mechanical sealing within the engine block is sound. If coolant were leaking directly into the combustion chamber (a classic "blown" gasket scenario), you would see a significant drop in compression on those specific cylinders. The water would occupy volume, displace air-fuel mixture, and potentially wash oil off cylinder walls, leading to misfires and erratic compression readings. Since your numbers are uniform and healthy, the internal combustion path is effectively closed.

The cooling system pressure loss, however, tells a different story. Modern cooling systems operate under pressure, typically between 13 and 15 psi, which raises the boiling point of coolant from 212Â°F to roughly 240Â°F or higher. When you lose this pressure without an external leak, the fluid is escaping internally. The most common culprit in your case is likely a compromised head gasket sealing the cylinder head to the engine block, but not allowing gas to escape into the cylindersâinstead, it allows coolant to migrate into the oil sump or evaporate through microscopic cracks near the expansion tank connection caused by thermal stress.

The fact that you had to top up the overflow tank after three weeks of sitting suggests a slow seepage rather than a catastrophic failure. This is often exacerbated by the history of overheating. When an engine overheats, the metal components (aluminum head and iron block) expand at different rates. Once the engine cools down completely, it contracts. If the thermal excursion was severe enough to warp the cylinder head or crack the gasket seal, you can end up with a situation where gas cannot escape into the cylinders (preserving compression) but coolant can migrate out of the cooling jacket into the crankcase via the PCV system or simply through the compromised gasket path.

To diagnose this without disassembly, perform a chemical analysis of your oil. If the head gasket is leaking coolant into the engine, you will find milky, frothy sludge on the dipstick and inside the crankcase ventilation system. This emulsion happens because water mixes with oil, breaking down its lubricating properties. You can also use a block tester, which detects combustion gases in the coolant overflow tank; a positive result confirms a breach between the cylinders and the cooling system.

If the compression test is clean but pressure decays in the radiator, the issue is almost certainly an external seal failure (like a water pump gasket or hose clamp) or a very specific internal migration path that hasn't yet flooded a cylinder. Given the history of belt failure and overheating, inspect the thermostat housing and water pump mounting surfaces for warping or cracking before assuming the head gasket itself is destroyed. Replacing the belt solved the immediate mechanical drive issue, but it didn't address the thermal damage already inflicted on the sealing surfaces.

If you proceed with repairs, ensure you replace the timing belt again if the first one failed due to age or tension issues, as this is a critical safety component in an interference engine like many Mazda MX-5s. Ignoring the pressure loss risk could lead to boiling coolant and catastrophic head warping over time. While some online forums might suggest simpler fixes, the physics of high-pressure cooling systems versus low-pressure combustion chambers makes this a clear case of internal leakage that warrants a thorough inspection of the oil system first.
